lesson.title: La Musique, Le Cinéma & Le Livre
lesson.subtitle: Talking about arts, cinema, books, and passions with aimer and préférer.

hook.title: Cultural Passions: La Musique, Le Cinéma & Les Livres
hook.content: Because aimer ('to like/love'), adorer ('to adore'), and préférer ('to prefer') talk about a passion as a whole category, they ALWAYS take the definite article le, la, l', les: J'aime la musique ('I love music'), J'adore le cinéma ('I love cinema'), Je préfère les livres ('I prefer books')!

footnotes.title: Why 'le livre' is a book, 'la librairie' is a bookshop, and 'la bibliothèque' is a library
footnotes.content: Latin liber ('book') gave French le livre and la librairie ('bookshop'), while Greek bibliothēkē gave French la bibliothèque ('lending library')!

pattern.title: aimer / adorer / préférer + le / la / l' / les
pattern.content: Always include the definite article when talking about your cultural passions.
pattern.linguist_note: Generic objects of verbs of appreciation require definite determiners in French.
pattern.trap_note: Never drop la or le in 'I love music and cinema' (*J'aime musique et cinéma) — always say J'aime la musique et le cinéma!

exercises.prompt: Match each cultural passion phrase with its French equivalent:

matching_pairs.english: I prefer the movies / cinema (definite le!)

exercises.target_answer: J'aime la musique, Je préfère le cinéma, un bon livre, au cinéma, à la librairie
exercises.meaning: I love music (definite la!), I prefer the movies / cinema (definite le!), a good book (masculine le livre), at the cinema (à + le), at the bookshop (false friend!)
exercises.explanation: Passions always wear their definite article after aimer and préférer.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I like music and French cinema'?
options: J'aime la musique et le cinéma français
J'aime de la musique et du cinéma français
exercises.target_answer: J'aime la musique et le cinéma français
exercises.meaning: aimer always takes definite la musique and le cinéma
exercises.explanation: Never leave nouns bare or use partitives after aimer.

exercises.prompt: Translate 'I prefer the book' using 'Je préfère' + 'the book':

exercises.idea: we are going to the cinema tonight because I love this movie (use ce film)
cues: We go to the cinema tonight → On va au cinéma ce soir
because I love this movie → parce que j'aime ce film
idea_parts: plan → On va au cinéma ce soir
reason → parce que j'aime ce film
exercises.target_answer: On va au cinéma ce soir parce que j'aime ce film
exercises.meaning: We're going to the cinema tonight because I love this movie
exercises.explanation: au cinéma (à + le) + parce que j'aime ce film.

diagnosis.cue: Fuse à + le into au cinéma.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: J'ai acheté un bon livre à la librairie
exercises.target_answer: J'ai acheté un bon livre à la librairie
exercises.meaning: I bought a good book at the bookshop
exercises.explanation: un bon livre (masculine) + à la librairie (bookshop).
exercises.affirmation: You paired un bon livre and à la librairie cleanly.

summary.outcome: Discuss music, cinema, books, and passions using mandatory definite articles after aimer, adorer, and préférer.

use_example.german: J'adore la musique, mais ce soir je préfère lire un bon livre.
use_example.english: I love music, but tonight I prefer to read a good book.

summary.takeaway: After aimer/adorer/préférer, always keep le, la, l', les (J'aime la musique).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([5151] La Tête, La Main & Le Cœur): see how La Musique, Le Cinéma & Le Livre leads directly into La Tête, La Main & Le Cœur.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "We're going to the cinema tonight because I love this movie" in French:
twist.target_answer: On va au cinéma ce soir parce que j'aime ce film
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "On va au cinéma ce soir parce que j'aime ce film" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of La Musique, Le Cinéma & Le Livre.

cinéma.context_phrase: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
cinéma.context_translation: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?
cinéma.etymology_derivation: Invented by the Lumière brothers in Lyon in 1895.

livre.etymology_derivation: Masculine le livre is 'the book'; feminine la livre is 'the pound'!

histoire.etymology_derivation: One French word covers both 'history' and 'story'.

aimé.etymology_derivation: aimer ← ad + estimare 'to estimate'. English 'aim' drifted from the same estimate — aiming is assessing.

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

voir.context_translation: I'm going to see my friend.
voir.etymology_derivation: Latin vidēre lost its middle d: vedere → veoir → voir.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
